title: Sikhism: one creator
hookLine: the Guru Granth Sahib opens with the Mool Mantar: one creator, truth is the name (Japji)

lines: A HOLY BOOK THAT STARTS WITH A NUMBER.
cards: The Sikh scripture begins with a number. Before a single word, on the very first page, there's the numeral one, written in Gurmukhi, the Punjabi script.
You'll see that symbol everywhere in Sikh life: over the doors of gurdwaras, on car dashboards, on pendants, even tattooed on forearms. It comes before everything else the Gurus have to say.
Today: Ik Onkar, and the few lines that follow it.

teach.b: Sikhism begins with Guru Nanak, born in Punjab, in what is now Pakistan.
Sikh tradition says that as a young man he disappeared into a river for three days and came out with a message about one God, and spent the rest of his life traveling and singing it.
His words, and those of the Gurus after him and of other saints, were gathered into the Guru Granth Sahib, which Sikhs honor as their living Guru.

teach.h: THE MOOL MANTAR: THE ROOT VERSE.
teach.b: It opens with the Mool Mantar, the root verse. Here is its sense, line by line; the Punjabi is compact, so this is a paraphrase. Ik Onkar: there is one creator, one being, present in everything.
Sat Naam: whose name is truth. Karta Purakh: the creator.
Nirbhau: without fear. Nirvair: without hate. Akal Murat: beyond time.
Ajuni: never born. Saibhang: existing by itself. Gur Prasad: known by the Guru's grace.
Nine short phrases, and a whole picture of God.
Ik is the numeral one, written as a digit, not spelled out; some readers see in that a way of leaving no room for doubt.
Onkar is a name for the one reality, and some read the long curving line drawn over the top as that oneness reaching on without end.
Sikhs say this one creator isn't far off: the same one is in every person, which is why Sikh teaching insists on the equality of all people, whatever their caste, gender or faith.
The Mool Mantar opens Japji Sahib, the prayer Sikhs who keep the daily prayers recite each morning.

how: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib, which begins with the Mool Mantar, early each morning, and the Ik Onkar symbol appears over gurdwara doors, in homes and on the first page of the Guru Granth Sahib.

games.q: you're writing the first word of a holy book about one God. how do you write it?
o: write the numeral one, as a digit.
games.why: the Guru Granth Sahib opens with the numeral one, joined to Onkar: ੴ.

practice: Draw the numeral one slowly, with a pen on a scrap of paper or with your finger on your palm, and breathe out as you draw, letting the word one settle in you.
Then picture the people you'll see today, one by one, and hold the thought that the same one is in each of them.

wordCard.voice: Ik Onkar. One creator: the numeral one that opens the Sikh scripture, the first words of the Mool Mantar. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the numeral one joined to Onkar, one creator.

carryVoice: Your line: one. One creator, and the same one in everyone. That's two hundred seventy-four days.
